paragraphs: Representation alignment trains a generative model by encouraging its internal features to resemble those of a pretrained teacher. For audio flow matching, choosing which layers receive this supervision matters substantially. AG-REPA investigates that choice instead of relying on a layer’s depth as a heuristic.

The paper identifies a distinction between storing useful information and influencing generation. A layer can closely resemble the teacher’s semantic or acoustic representations without contributing strongly to the velocity field that guides audio generation. The proposed forward-only gate ablation measures each layer’s contribution through the change it induces in the predicted velocity field. These measurements determine a sparse selection of layers and adapt how strongly each receives alignment supervision.

Across joint speech and general-audio training with different arrangements of token conditioning, AG-REPA consistently improves over REPA baselines. The findings support selecting supervision targets according to their measured functional influence: representational similarity alone does not identify the layers where alignment most effectively improves generation.
icml-2026-ag-repa-causal-layer-selection.tldr: AG-REPA improves audio representation alignment by supervising layers according to their measured causal contribution to generation.

paragraphs: An AI agent’s confidence needs to reflect whether its entire task execution succeeded. This is harder than assessing a single answer because errors can accumulate across steps, tools introduce uncertainty, and the reason for failure may be difficult to see. The paper introduces agentic confidence calibration as a distinct problem.

Its proposed framework, Holistic Trajectory Calibration, examines information from the agent’s full execution history. It extracts process features ranging from broad trajectory behavior to fine-grained stability, then uses a simple, interpretable model to estimate confidence. This makes the process that produced an answer part of the assessment and exposes signals associated with failure.

Across eight benchmarks, multiple language models, and different agent frameworks, HTC improves both calibration and the ability to distinguish success from failure over strong baselines. The authors also report transfer across domains without retraining. Their General Agent Calibrator achieves the lowest expected calibration error on the out-of-domain GAIA evaluation, supporting the usefulness of execution-level evidence for assessing agent reliability.
icml-2026-agentic-confidence-calibration.tldr: Holistic Trajectory Calibration uses an agent’s execution history to estimate confidence and reveal signals of failure.

paragraphs: Recommendation systems often learn from sparse user interactions, making it difficult to find solutions that generalize well. Recursive Self-Improving Recommendation addresses this shortage by using the current model to generate additional training material. The framework does not require external data or a separate teacher model.

Each iteration generates plausible sequences of user interactions and checks their fidelity to an approximate representation of the user’s preferences. Only sequences that pass this quality control enrich the dataset used to train a successor model. The filtering step is central: it connects synthetic examples to the preferences the system is trying to learn. The theoretical analysis describes this process as implicit regularization that smooths the optimization landscape and encourages more robust solutions.

Experiments show cumulative improvements across several benchmarks and architectures, including smaller models. The authors also find that weaker models can produce useful training curricula for stronger ones. These results support recursive, quality-controlled data generation as an approach to recommendation sparsity, with broader applications presented as a possible direction.
icml-2026-can-recommender-systems-teach-.tldr: RSIR improves recommendation models through repeated generation, preference-consistency filtering, and training on enriched interaction data.

paragraphs: Code2Worlds uses coding language models to turn language into simulation code for three-dimensional worlds that change over time. The paper addresses two obstacles: coordinating detailed objects with the overall environment, and producing dynamics that behave physically rather than merely looking plausible.

The framework separates object creation from environmental organization. One stream generates objects with retrieval support, while another organizes the environment hierarchically. It then introduces a feedback loop for motion: a PostProcess Agent writes dynamics, and a vision-language motion critic assesses the result and guides repeated code refinement. This connects code generation to an explicit review of the simulated behavior.

On the Code4D benchmark, the authors report a 41% gain in SGS and 49% higher Richness relative to baselines. They also report physics-aware dynamics that prior static methods do not generate. The contribution combines scene organization with iterative dynamics refinement, extending coding-based world generation beyond static environments while evaluating both scene quality and the presence of physical motion.
icml-2026-code2worlds-empowering-coding-.tldr: Code2Worlds combines structured scene generation with a physics-aware feedback loop to produce simulation code for dynamic 3D worlds.

paragraphs: Visuo-tactile sensors support robotic manipulation, but differences in their designs make it difficult to learn representations that work across sensors. Training based on reconstruction or individual tasks can miss the information sensors share, especially when their outputs differ substantially. CTSRL addresses this problem with a unified tactile representation framework.

A Cross-Sensor Modulator targets sensor-specific biases, and training proceeds in two stages. First, aligned synthetic data provides self-supervised learning across sensor domains, encouraging a shared internal representation. Second, real-world multimodal tactile data connects these learned features to richer semantic information through cross-modal alignment. This stage is designed to bridge the semantic gap between simulated and real observations.

The experiments report strong generalization across multiple sensors and substantial improvement in sensor-agnostic representation learning. The approach matters because it explicitly addresses both sources of variation: differences among sensor designs and differences between synthetic and real data. Its reported results support learning common tactile information while retaining fine-grained semantic attributes useful for interpreting touch.
icml-2026-cross-tactile-sensor-represent.tldr: CTSRL combines aligned synthetic training and real multimodal alignment to learn tactile representations that generalize across sensor designs.

paragraphs: Robots can use demonstrations of familiar tasks as context when attempting unfamiliar tasks without updating model parameters. However, demonstrations expressed only as continuous action sequences may encourage copying trajectories without identifying reusable skills. Decompose and Recompose introduces an intermediate representation that pairs individual skills with the actions that implement them.

The framework breaks demonstrations into interpretable skill–action alignments, then uses those pieces to reason about new combinations and execution order. It builds a task-specific demonstration library through visual-semantic retrieval and skill sequences supplied by a planning agent. A separate static library emphasizes skill coverage, supplying patterns that the dynamically retrieved demonstrations may lack.

Together, the libraries provide demonstrations intended to cover the skills needed for compositional reasoning. Experiments on AGNOSTOS and in real-world environments validate zero-shot generalization across tasks. The stated result supports making skill structure explicit in demonstration context, so that previously observed abilities can inform new task execution without treating an entire demonstrated trajectory as the reusable unit.
icml-2026-decompose-and-recompose-reason.tldr: Decompose and Recompose organizes demonstrations into skill–action pairs that robots can recombine for unseen manipulation tasks.

paragraphs: Aligning diffusion language models requires policy optimization suited to their generation process. A costly part is calculating probabilities along the sequence of intermediate diffusion states. dTRPO reduces this calculation to make larger-scale offline policy training more practical.

The paper establishes two trajectory reductions. Under reference policy regularization, the probability ratio for newly unmasked tokens is an unbiased estimate of the ratio for intermediate diffusion states. It also shows that full-trajectory probability can be effectively estimated using one forward pass on a final state that has been masked again. These results support an optimization objective that avoids evaluating the full trajectory in the usual way.

Evaluations on 7B diffusion language models report gains of up to 9.6% on STEM tasks, 4.3% on coding, and 3.0% on instruction following. These are maximum reported gains rather than uniform improvements across every task. The authors also report strong training efficiency from offline, single-forward computation and improved generation efficiency associated with higher-quality outputs, linking the probability reductions to practical training and generation benefits.
icml-2026-dtrpo-trajectory-reduction-in-.tldr: dTRPO reduces diffusion-language-model trajectory calculations to enable efficient offline policy training and improve reasoning and instruction following.

paragraphs: Vision-language-action policies may fail when their surroundings change because their decisions depend on visual cues unrelated to the task. This paper investigates that possibility by treating visual attribution as an intervention problem: estimating how changing the available visual information affects predicted actions.

The Interventional Significance Score uses masking interventions to estimate the causal influence of image regions. The Nuisance Mass Ratio then summarizes how much attribution falls on task-irrelevant features. The authors analyze ISS statistically, showing that it admits unbiased estimation. They also characterize conditions under which action prediction error can serve as a valid proxy for causal influence, so that connection is explicitly conditional.

Across varied manipulation tasks, the experiments indicate that NMR predicts generalization behavior and that ISS produces more faithful explanations than existing interpretability methods. These findings suggest a diagnostic use: examining which visual features drive actions can help identify policies whose apparent competence depends on irrelevant cues. The reported contribution is a way to detect such misalignment, with empirical evidence connecting the diagnostic to generalization.
icml-2026-embodied-interpretability-link.tldr: Interventional visual attribution helps diagnose whether robot policies rely on task-irrelevant cues associated with poor generalization.

paragraphs: Text-to-image diffusion models can generate compelling scenes while struggling with readable lettering, especially in dense or multiline layouts and scripts such as Chinese. FreeText improves text rendering without retraining by using mechanisms already present in diffusion transformers. It separates locating text from shaping the characters themselves.

To locate writing regions, the method extracts spatial information associated with individual tokens from image-to-text attention. It uses sink-like tokens as stable anchors and refines the resulting regions into confident masks. To shape characters, Spectral-Modulated Glyph Injection introduces a noise-aligned glyph prior whose frequency content is filtered. This strengthens letter structure and reduces cases where the model depicts a word’s meaning instead of writing the word.

Experiments cover Qwen-Image, FLUX.1-dev, and SD3 variants across three text-rendering benchmarks. The authors report consistent readability improvements while preserving semantic alignment and aesthetic quality, with modest inference overhead. The findings support addressing placement and glyph structure separately within an existing generator, making accurate text rendering more accessible without an additional training stage.
icml-2026-freetext-training-free-text-re.tldr: FreeText improves generated text without retraining by finding writing regions through attention and injecting frequency-filtered glyph structure.

paragraphs: GeoMoLa learns compact, discrete representations of robot motion by predicting how three-dimensional point clouds change during manipulation. Its training objective focuses on spatial geometry evolving over time. This directs the learned codes toward the physical effects of movement, instead of making visual reconstruction the central learning task.

The method uses a single RGB-D view and achieves state-of-the-art results across diverse manipulation benchmarks, where existing approaches require multiview reconstruction. Ablation experiments identify geometric prediction as the key contributor to performance. The authors also apply learned codes to new scenes and observe physically consistent transformations across different visual contexts, providing evidence that the codes capture reusable motion patterns.

Real-world experiments report robust manipulation with few demonstrations in cluttered environments where geometry matters for success. Together, these findings support predicting motion’s three-dimensional consequences as a useful way to learn action abstractions. The reported transfer across scenes connects the representation objective to practical robustness: the same motion code can retain a meaningful physical effect when the surrounding appearance changes.
icml-2026-geomola-geometry-aware-motion-.tldr: GeoMoLa learns reusable robot motion codes by predicting changing 3D geometry, achieving robust manipulation from single-view RGB-D input.

paragraphs: Learning rates are sensitive tuning choices, and selecting them repeatedly becomes expensive as networks grow deeper. Existing maximal-update parametrization helps explain transfer across network width. This paper extends the analysis of learning-rate scaling across depth for non-recurrent architectures with multiple computational paths, including CNNs, ResNets, and Transformers.

The authors define effective depth in a way that depends on architecture. It counts sequential units that contribute updates while absorbing fixed local structure into constants. Under stabilizing initializations and a maximal-update criterion, they derive a shared leading-order rule: the base learning-rate scale decreases with effective depth to the power of minus three-halves. The update budget concerns typical representation changes from one step at initialization.

Experiments across different architectures confirm the predicted slope and support learning-rate transfer across both depth and width without retuning the destination model. The significance is a common scaling rule expressed through architecture-aware depth. Its theoretical scope remains tied to the stated initialization and update conditions, and to leading-order behavior as effective depth grows.
icml-2026-hyperparameter-transfer-laws-f.tldr: Under stated initialization and update conditions, a shared effective-depth scaling law enables learning-rate transfer across several network architectures.

paragraphs: Cross-view geo-localization identifies a location by matching ground or drone imagery with satellite views. Differences in regional appearance and weather make this difficult, and drone images add clutter from many small objects. InfoGeo addresses these challenges by focusing on object-centered structure rather than relying solely on whole-image feature alignment.

The framework casts learning as an information bottleneck with two complementary goals. It preserves information shared across viewpoints by aligning structural relationships among objects. It also suppresses viewpoint-specific noise using constraints that share knowledge across views. The intended representation therefore emphasizes relationships that remain useful for matching while reducing dependence on appearance signals that change between observations.

Evaluations across multiple benchmarks and challenging scenarios show significant improvements over state-of-the-art methods. These results support the framework’s use of object relations and information filtering for more robust cross-view matching. The practical motivation is localization and navigation where GPS is unavailable: useful visual correspondence must survive changes in viewpoint and surrounding conditions, even when a drone image contains substantial fine-grained clutter.
icml-2026-infogeo-information-theoretic-.tldr: InfoGeo improves cross-view geo-localization by preserving shared object relationships and suppressing viewpoint-specific visual noise.

paragraphs: Planning-based reinforcement learning often selects actions through sampling methods such as Model Predictive Path Integral optimization. MPPI supports broad exploration, but its updates do not use the smooth return gradients available in structured dynamics. This paper introduces Langevin Rollout Optimization to add gradient-guided refinement to action planning.

LaRO uses Langevin dynamics to refine action sequences through return gradients while retaining exploration across multiple promising regions. A world model learns both dynamics and a score function in a shared latent space, supporting efficient gradient estimates for real-time planning. Maximum Look-Ahead Planning then combines LaRO with MPPI through a choice mechanism, bringing both planners into the same system.

The authors incorporate this combined planner into BOOM, producing BOOM-L. On the DeepMind Control Suite and Humanoid Bench, BOOM-L consistently exceeds strong baselines in sample efficiency and final performance. The results support combining sampling-based exploration with gradient-guided local refinement, with the learned score-augmented world model supplying the information needed to make that refinement practical.
icml-2026-langevin-rollout-optimization-.tldr: LaRO adds gradient-guided action refinement to sampling-based planning, improving control performance and sample efficiency in BOOM-L.

paragraphs: Memory-based test-time adaptation uses incoming examples to improve later predictions when the data distribution changes. However, assigning each example to a single class using a model’s own prediction can store mistakes that bias future decisions. Limited memory capacity creates another problem when eviction discards informative examples.

A²Memory addresses class assignment through representations built from diverse visual attributes shared across classes. It uses these textual representations and soft assignment to construct surrogate visual representations, reducing reliance on a single predicted label. Its associative memory then compresses the incoming stream into fixed capacity through gradient-based optimization and data-dependent retention. Retrieval produces class prototypes adapted to the current sample.

Experiments across 15 benchmarks show consistent improvements over state-of-the-art methods. The framework’s contribution is to treat both memory construction and retention as parts of adaptation that need careful design. Its results support using attribute information to handle uncertain assignments and learned compression to preserve useful information within a bounded memory, improving subsequent predictions under distribution shift.
icml-2026-learning-to-memorize-with-attr.tldr: A²Memory improves online adaptation through attribute-based soft assignment and learned compression of a fixed-capacity memory.

paragraphs: Sentence embeddings compress sentence meaning into a representation usable by language-processing applications. Many LLM-based methods extract final-layer hidden states, although those states are optimized for predicting the next token. This paper finds that attention value vectors provide a better source of sentence-level semantic information.

Value Aggregation pools token values across multiple layers and token positions without additional training. The authors then develop Aligned Weighted Value Aggregation using an interpretation that holds with suitable prompts: the final token’s attention scores weight the value vectors, and the attention output projection aligns them with the model’s shared residual-stream space. This turns attention outputs into an aligned, weighted representation for aggregation.

In training-free evaluations, basic Value Aggregation beats other LLM embeddings and matches or exceeds the ensemble-based MetaEOL. AlignedWVA achieves state-of-the-art performance among training-free LLM embeddings and surpasses MetaEOL by a substantial margin. The paper also highlights fine-tuning Value Aggregation as a promising route to stronger embedding models, extending the idea beyond its demonstrated training-free use.
icml-2026-llm-based-embeddings-attention.tldr: Aggregating attention value vectors produces stronger training-free sentence embeddings, with further gains from attention weighting and output-space alignment.

paragraphs: Physics-informed neural networks can solve fluid equations without a mesh, but enforcing equations point by point can struggle in complex, winding geometries. Local constraints may fail to connect information across channels, leading to unstable gradients and violations of conservation. MUSA-PINN addresses this through constraints defined over regions.

The method expresses the Navier–Stokes constraints as integral conservation laws over spherical control volumes. It measures continuity and momentum through flux balance on their surfaces. Three scales serve different purposes: large volumes connect distant regions, intermediate volumes follow transport pathways, and small volumes refine local behavior. A two-stage training schedule gives priority to continuity.

Experiments focus on steady incompressible flow in triply periodic minimal-surface geometries. In that setting, MUSA-PINN outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, reduces relative errors by up to 93%, and preserves mass conservation. The results support combining conservation over finite regions with multiple spatial scales, allowing the learning objective to reflect both local flow detail and the longer-range connections imposed by tortuous channels.
icml-2026-musa-pinn-multi-scale-weak-for.tldr: MUSA-PINN enforces fluid conservation across multiple spatial scales to improve flow prediction in complex channel geometries.

paragraphs: Generating physical systems requires samples that satisfy the governing partial differential equations as well as resemble the target data. Diffusion methods face a difficulty during stochastic denoising: enforcing constraints on the expected clean sample introduces a Jensen’s Gap, creating a trade-off between physical consistency and generation accuracy.

Physics-Informed Distillation of Diffusion Models addresses this with a post-training distillation stage that enforces PDE constraints. The resulting model generates samples in a single step while improving physical consistency and sample quality. The framework supports forward problems, inverse problems, and reconstruction when only partial observations are available, connecting the same distillation strategy to several physical modeling tasks.

Across PDE benchmarks, PIDDM outperforms PIDM, DiffusionPDE, and ECI-sampling in both accuracy and constraint satisfaction. The authors also report lower computation and little hyperparameter tuning. These findings indicate that the reported gains in physical fidelity do not require sacrificing sample accuracy in the tested settings, while single-step generation makes the distilled model computationally more efficient.
icml-2026-physics-informed-distillation-.tldr: PIDDM distills diffusion models into single-step generators that improve both sample accuracy and satisfaction of physical equations.

paragraphs: Score-based diffusion models encounter a mathematical bottleneck in Bayesian inverse problems: the time-dependent likelihood score is difficult to evaluate analytically. Proximal-based generative modeling develops an alternative sampling framework that avoids explicit likelihood evaluation, using a connection between diffusion and nonsmooth optimization.

The framework rests on a theoretical equivalence between Gaussian convolution and Moreau–Yosida regularization. From this connection, the authors define a Moreau score with a closed-form expression in terms of proximal operators. They also introduce Moreau score matching to learn these operators using only samples from the prior distribution. This provides a way to train the components needed by the new sampler without requiring explicit likelihood evaluation.

The theoretical results establish non-asymptotic convergence and elimination of the early-stopping bias identified in score-based diffusion. Experiments show significant gains over state-of-the-art methods in reconstruction quality and sampling time. The contribution therefore combines a different mathematical route to sampling with reported practical benefits, addressing both the likelihood-score obstacle and the efficiency of solving inverse problems.
icml-2026-proximal-based-generative-mode.tldr: PGM uses learned proximal operators to sample for Bayesian inverse problems without explicit likelihood evaluation, improving reconstruction and speed.

paragraphs: Adapting a language model to different user preferences through additional training can require expensive data preparation and computation. REAR explores adaptation during inference instead. It treats the problem as realignment because a base model may respond to a question without adequately reflecting the preference supplied alongside it.

The framework separates the underlying reward into a question-related component and a preference-related component. Its realignment reward selectively changes the balance between them. The authors show that this reward can be expressed as a linear combination of token-level policy log-probabilities, making it computationally convenient to use with methods such as best-of-N sampling and tree search.

Experiments report scalable preference realignment across diverse user requirements compared with other test-time approaches. They also show transfer to mathematical and visual tasks when appropriate preferences are specified. The contribution is a reward construction that makes inference-time search sensitive to the desired balance between answering the question and following user preferences, extending test-time scaling beyond settings organized primarily around verifiable correctness.
icml-2026-rear-test-time-preference-real.tldr: REAR rebalances question and preference rewards during inference to improve preference alignment without additional model training.

paragraphs: Implicit neural representations offer a continuous representation for MRI reconstruction, but optimizing a new model from scratch for every scan takes time. IPOD learns an initialization that can adapt rapidly to a scan, addressing this computational burden without relying on fully sampled reference images during meta-learning.

The framework learns directly from undersampled measurements across reconstruction tasks with different sampling patterns. This variation is used to capture a prior that generalizes across tasks. An adaptive meta-update strategy changes the learning update according to task-specific performance, with the aim of producing suitable initial parameters for diverse anatomical structures.

Experiments report faster adaptation and high-fidelity reconstruction across several imaging protocols, substantially outperforming existing implicit-representation baselines. The stated findings link the learned initialization to both efficiency and reconstruction quality. Removing the need for fully sampled training references also changes the data requirements of meta-learning, supporting the authors’ proposal of a scalable approach to imaging inverse problems while retaining scan-specific adaptation as part of reconstruction.
icml-2026-reference-free-meta-learning-f.tldr: IPOD learns MRI reconstruction initializations directly from undersampled data, enabling rapid adaptation without fully sampled training references.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards can improve language-model reasoning, but generating training rollouts and collecting reward signals is expensive. This paper examines how much training data is needed and how to concentrate computation on examples that are especially informative for policy updates.

The authors establish a theoretical lower bound on the sample complexity required to unlock reasoning capabilities. Separately, their empirical results show that strong performance can arise from surprisingly few training instances. They introduce Dynamic One-Shot Policy Refinement, which selects a single informative sample from each batch. Selection is uncertainty-aware and uses reward volatility together with exploration-driven acquisition to guide which sample receives the update.

DoPR reduces rollout overhead by nearly an order of magnitude while retaining competitive reasoning accuracy. The result supports dynamically selecting training examples as a practical way to reduce reinforcement-learning costs. Its efficiency claim combines sparse policy updates with informative sample selection; it does not require treating every available training instance as equally valuable at every stage of learning.
icml-2026-resource-efficient-reinforceme.tldr: DoPR selects one informative sample per batch, cutting rollout overhead by nearly an order of magnitude while preserving competitive reasoning accuracy.

paragraphs: Vision-language reasoning can fail before reasoning properly begins if the model describes the image incorrectly. Training based only on final-answer correctness can spend substantial computation on these unsuccessful paths and cannot clearly separate perception errors from reasoning errors. MIRL addresses both problems by treating perception and reasoning separately.

The framework uses mutual information between a generated description and the image as an inexpensive screening signal. It directs further sampling toward promising descriptions through trajectory forking. During training, independent mutual-information rewards also provide feedback for the perception stage, giving visual understanding its own optimization signal instead of relying exclusively on the final answer.

Across six vision-language reasoning benchmarks, MIRL reaches 70.22% average accuracy. The reported configuration uses 10 preliminary samples with top-6 selection and outperforms sampling 16 complete trajectories while using 25% fewer complete trajectories. These findings support checking visual grounding early: screening can improve where computation is spent, while separate perception rewards help address the ambiguity of a single correctness signal.
icml-2026-see-first-reason-later-mutual-.tldr: MIRL screens visual descriptions and rewards perception separately, improving vision-language reasoning while reducing complete-trajectory sampling.

paragraphs: Point clouds come from sources with very different geometries, densities, and underlying patterns. Utonia explores whether one self-supervised point transformer encoder can learn across this diversity. Its training spans remote sensing, outdoor LiDAR, indoor RGB-D sequences, object-centered CAD data, and point clouds derived from RGB-only videos.

The model learns a shared representation space that transfers across these domains. Joint training improves perception and produces behaviors the authors observe only when the domains are trained together. This makes the combination of heterogeneous data part of the contribution: the aim is a representation that benefits from differences among sources while remaining useful across them.

The authors also test uses beyond perception. Adding Utonia features to vision-language-action policies improves robotic manipulation, while integrating them into vision-language models improves spatial reasoning. These observations support the broader usefulness of its 3D representations. The paper presents Utonia as an initial step toward foundation models for sparse 3D data, with AR/VR, robotics, and autonomous driving identified as potential application areas.
icml-2026-utonia-toward-one-encoder-for-.tldr: Utonia jointly learns from diverse point-cloud domains, producing transferable features that also improve manipulation and spatial reasoning.

paragraphs: Models increasingly train on synthetic examples produced by earlier models, creating feedback loops that can amplify bias or destabilize learning. Prior analysis of a single model consuming its own outputs found that human curation could steer alignment. This paper examines what happens when several models instead learn from one another’s generated input-output pairs.

The authors formalize interacting self-consuming models as a dynamical system and characterize when it converges to a stable point. They distinguish the effect of curating a model’s data on that model’s alignment from the effects that propagate to other models. This separates direct influence from the changes transmitted through the wider training loop.

The analysis shows that interactions can weaken or even reverse the alignment benefits of human curation, potentially worsening long-term alignment. The claim is conditional on cross-model dynamics, rather than a claim that curation generally fails. Its significance is that a locally beneficial intervention may behave differently inside an interconnected training system, making the relationships among models relevant to understanding the eventual outcome.
icml-2026-when-and-how-human-curation-ba.tldr: In interacting synthetic-data training loops, cross-model feedback can weaken or reverse the alignment benefits of human curation.

paragraphs: Language-model safety is uneven across languages, with languages that have fewer resources receiving weaker protection. This paper investigates the internal mechanisms behind safety transfer and identifies a small set of neurons shared across languages that plays a critical role in refusal behavior.

The authors first identify safety-related neurons within individual languages and test their causal role through targeted activation and suppression. They then locate neurons shared between high-resource and non-high-resource languages. Suppressing this shared subset reduces safety across several non-high-resource languages at once, while reinforcing it improves cross-language defensive consistency. These interventions provide evidence that the shared neurons help connect safety behavior across languages.

Building on those findings, the paper proposes training that targets the shared subset according to language-resource distribution and model architecture. Experiments show that fine-tuning this small group outperforms state-of-the-art methods, improves safety in non-high-resource languages, and maintains general capabilities. The contribution links a mechanistic finding to a focused training intervention, with reported benefits extending across the evaluated languages.
icml-2026-who-transfers-safety-identifyi.tldr: Targeting a small set of shared safety neurons improves safety across non-high-resource languages while preserving general model capabilities.
